full_judgment: 43. In the instant case, the charge-sheet was: submitted on 17.8.1996, i.e. 80 days after the F.I.R., lodged on 29.5.1996. Ne. doubt the-charge-sheet was submitted well within time but during .trial none of the prosecution witnesses could go any-where near to say anything in support of the prosecution case, nakedly revealing the hollowness of the entire investigation. However, it appears that on receipt of the records of the G.R. No. 302 of 1996 (Sundaiganj) from the relevant court of the Magistrate, Gaibandha, for trial, the Nari-Q-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Bishesh Adalat, Gaibandha, under Section 17 of the Act, took cognizance on 27.8.1996 of the offence under the provision of Section 6(4) and 14 of the Act against 10 (ten) accused persons including the condemned prisoner. The word 'cognizance' was not defined any where in the Code. In Gopal Vs. Emperor, AIR (30) 1943 Pat 245, it was observed that the word 'cognizance' is used in the Code to indicate the point when the Magistrate or a Judge first takes judicial notice of an offence. It is a different thing from the initiation of proceedings. It is the condition precedent to the initiation of proceedings by the Magistrate. The Supreme Court of India, while considering the question of taking cognizance has, in the case of R.R. Chart Vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh AIR 1951 SC 207, approved the following observations by Das Gupta, J. made in the case of Superintendent and Remembrancer of Legal Affairs, West Bengal Vs. Abani Kumar Banerji, AIR 1950 Cal 437 : "What is "taking cognizance" has not been defined in the Criminal Procedure Code and I have no desire now to attempt to define it. It seems to me clear, however, that before it can be said that any Magistrate has taken cognizance of any offence under S.190(1)(a), Criminal P.C. he must not only have applied his mind to the con-tents of the petition but he must have done so for the purpose of proceeding in a particular way ..." This view of Das Gupta J. was again approved by the Supreme Court of India in the later case of Narayandas Bhagwandas Madhabdas Vs. The State of West Bengal AIR 1959 SC 1118 and also by a Full Bench of the Calcutta High Court in the case of A.K. Roy Vs. The State of West Bengal AIR 1962 Cal 135 where it was observed as follows: "Where it appears that a Magistrate has not only applied his mind to the facts of the case contained in a police report and the connected police papers, but desires to proceed with the trial of the case, he must be held to have taken cognizance of the case."
